query: For multicomponent high-entropy alloys in solid and liquid states at and near their high melting temperatures, what single testable methodological intervention could overcome the inability of EAM references to represent the many atomic configurations of the ab initio liquid? Explain why it should improve reference–target phase-space overlap, predict the reduction in thermodynamic-integration path mismatch relative to TOR-TILD’s EAM references, define the applicable composition and temperature ranges, identify supporting evidence from elemental or binary calculations, and specify a decisive free-energy benchmark that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Replacing traditional EAM reference potentials with an actively‐learned deep neural network (machine‐learned) interatomic potential tailored to capture the many-body interactions in complex atomic configurations of high‐entropy alloy liquids will improve phase-space overlap between the reference and ab initio target systems and thereby reduce the thermodynamic-integration path mismatch relative to TOR-TILD’s EAM references.
generation.material_initial_state: Multicomponent high-entropy alloys in solid and liquid states at high temperatures near their melting points (for example, refractory HEAs where T ≈ 0.9–1.1 Tm).
generation.intervention: Implement a deep-learning potential (DLP) generated via active learning from ab initio data as the reference potential in thermodynamic integration calculations, replacing the conventional EAM reference.
generation.conditions: The intervention is applicable for HEAs and complex concentrated alloys at high melting temperatures (e.g., refractory systems) where the liquid state shows significant configurational diversity. It targets conditions at or near the melting point (T/Tm around 0.9 to 1.1) and compositions where many local atomic environments coexist.
generation.structural_mediator: The many-body interactions and local atomic environment diversity encoded in the DLP serve as the structural mediator, fostering a reference ensemble that more accurately samples the liquid-phase configuration space.
generation.mechanism: Because deep learning potentials can be trained on extensive ab initio data covering a wide range of local environments, they more faithfully reproduce the potential energy surface of both solid and liquid phases. This enhanced flexibility ensures a tighter matching to the ab initio target ensemble, thereby minimizing the integration path mismatch during free energy calculations.
generation.predicted_outcome: A significant reduction in the thermodynamic integration path mismatch is expected compared to the TOR-TILD EAM reference, potentially reducing the mismatch by a factor on the order of a few times (e.g., 2–10× improvement), although the exact magnitude remains uncertain and will depend on the alloy system and training data quality.
generation.baseline: TOR-TILD calculations using standard EAM potentials, which insufficiently sample the full configurational diversity of the liquid phase and thereby show larger free energy integration path discrepancies.
generation.boundary: The method should be effective for HEAs where adequate ab initio training data can be generated and computational cost is manageable. It may be limited in cases where the chemical complexity or extreme conditions present challenges to generating a representative training set, or where the DLP may not capture very subtle effects beyond its training regime.
generation.uncertainty: The precise quantitative reduction in integration path mismatch is uncertain and will need to be calibrated via direct comparison. Variability is expected depending on the specific HEA composition, temperature regime, and the extent of ab initio data available for training the deep learning potential.

falsification_experiment.design: Select a representative high-entropy alloy system near its melting temperature. Compute its liquid-phase free energy via thermodynamic integration using (a) the standard TOR-TILD methodology with an EAM reference potential and (b) the same methodology with an actively learned deep neural network potential as the reference. Compare the integration path mismatch and convergence behavior between the two approaches.
measurements: Quantitative phase-space overlap metrics (e.g., overlap distribution statistics)
Convergence rates of integration parameters (e.g., path-length, variance)
Differences in predicted structural and energetic distributions versus ab initio benchmarks
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the use of the deep learning potential does not result in a statistically significant improvement in phase-space overlap or a notable reduction in the integration path mismatch—i.e., if convergence metrics and free-energy differences remain comparable to or worse than those obtained with the EAM-based TOR-TILD references—then the hypothesis is falsified.

Ab initio framework for deciphering trade-off relationships in multi-component alloys

Abstract: While first-principles methods have been successfully applied to characterize individual properties of multi-principal element alloys (MPEA), their use in searching for optimal trade-offs between competing properties is hampered by high computational demands. In this work, we present a framework to explore Pareto-optimal compositions by integrating advanced ab initio-based techniques into a Bayesian multi-objective optimization workflow, complemented by a simple analytical model providing straightforward analysis of trends. Melting simulations of high-entropy carbonitrides by deep learning potentials

Abstract: The melting temperature is a crucial property of materials that determines their potential applications in different industrial fields. In this study, we used a deep neural network potential to describe the structure of high-entropy (TiZrTaHfNb)CxN1−x carbonitrides (HECN) in both solid and liquid states. This approach allows us to predict heating and cooling temperatures depending on the nitrogen content to determine the melting temperature and analyze structure changes from atomistic point of view. A steady increase in nitrogen content leads to increasing melting temperature, with a maximum approaching for 25% of nitrogen in the HECN. A careful analysis of pair correlations, together with calculations of entropy in the considered liquid phases of HECNs allows us to explain the origin of the nonlinear enhancement of the melting temperature with increasing nitrogen content. The maximum melting temperature of 3580 ± 30 K belongs to (TiZrTaHfNb)C0.75N0.25 composition.
